extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy analysts studying gender bias in grant allocation, scientometricians, and social scientists interested in peer review methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary on replicating and correctly interpreting the Wennerås & Wold (1997) study on sexism and nepotism in peer review, focusing on methods for comparing competence scores, past performance, and gender in grant allocation. Emphasizes data access, choice of performance indicators, sample selection, and statistical model assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence Score (panel evaluation of track record)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wennerås & Wold study focused on the so called Competence Score which in the Swedish Medical Research Council more or less was how the panel evaluated the track record of each applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the panel's competence score (an explicit evaluation of track record) as the outcome of interest rather than coarse outcomes like funding success. The original method predicts competence score from past performance and gender; replication should preserve this central concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate success rates with competence scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Although often read in that way, the sexism and nepotism study never talked about success rates in grant allocation. The word “success” was even never mentioned in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misrepresenting the original study by analysing success rates when the original compared competence scores. Many follow-up studies have mistakenly treated W&W as a success-rate study; replicators should be explicit about which outcome they study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size-dependent performance indicator (sum of journal impact factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wennerås & Wold simply added the journal impact factors per publication into one measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using a size-dependent indicator (e.g., summing impact factors across publications) if matching the original approach. This enables certain regression analyses but also carries implicit assumptions about how publications should be aggregated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict competence score from past performance and gender (regression approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The core method was predicting the competence score from past performance and gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replications should model panel-assigned competence scores as a function of measurable past performance and applicant gender (e.g., via regression). Be explicit about the dependent variable and modelling choices to mirror or test the original claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection: focus on early-career / first-time applicants when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: W&W studied young researchers who applied more or less for the first time. They had just finished their post-doc period and applied for a fellowship. Basically men and women were on the same foot; their publication records were comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the original sample frame (early-career applicants) when attempting comparable inference; differences in career stage and prior publication records can confound gender effects if not controlled or if sample composition differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to peer evaluation data (panel scores and reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: To have full information about the peer’s evaluation of grant applications are seldom accessible for researchers to analyse. Public laws and data protection stand between the interest of the researcher and the interest of the council and/or the individual applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain the original panel evaluation data (scores, competence assessments) where possible. Lack of access to detailed peer-evaluation records forces studies to proxy with success rates and can lead to misinterpretation. Address legal/privacy constraints explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for academic rank and publication output
rubrics_metrics.description: Waisbren ... find that women and men are equally successful, and that only marginal differences occur after controlling for academic rank. Many studies find that scholarly production and impact is significantly higher for male applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include controls such as academic rank and quantitative publication/output measures to separate effects of productivity and status from evaluative bias. Be cautious interpreting funding differences without these controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and account for nepotism
rubrics_metrics.description: The competence score indicated favouring of women, but that was ‘corrected’ by nepotism in favour of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and adjust for nepotism/in-group favoritism where possible (e.g., network ties, institutional affiliations). Nepotism can mask or reverse apparent gender effects in aggregate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider plasticity of peer review and temporal/political changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The study indicated the plasticity of peer review – political pressure changed the valuation of track records. A plasticity which might be the main explanation as to why peer review continues to produce biased effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for changes over time and institutional pressures that may alter how track records are valued. Longitudinal analysis or sensitivity checks for periods of policy change are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine regression model assumptions (e.g., linearity) and test alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The regression models were criticised, as was the assumption of the linearity of the performance model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely unquestioningly on linear regression assumptions. Test model specification, non-linearity, interactions, and alternative modelling approaches; use robustness checks and consider alternative hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and public disclosure of data for reanalysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceci & Williams also made an important statement concerning the openness of research data. They said to be waiting for the public disclosure of the original Wennerås & Wold data in order to test possible other hypotheses, and apply other analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make data publicly available alongside publication when legally/ethically possible, to allow reanalysis and testing of alternative hypotheses. Planned replication in the blog promises to publish all data with the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicate using other methods, not only identical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: We agree with Ceci & Williams that it is worthwhile to replicate the study also with other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement direct replication with methodological variation (different indicators, models, or causal inference techniques) to test robustness of original findings and explore alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use performance measures that reflect what panels evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper has inspired a lot of research on gender bias in science, also the GRANteD project, as it was the first analysis that explicitly included past performance measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select bibliometric or performance indicators that align with the aspects of track record panels actually consider (e.g., quality-adjusted outputs, impact measures used by panels) rather than generic productivity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misrepresentation in citations and secondary literature
rubrics_metrics.description: If we consider all articles that cite the Waisbren study, we find that none but one paper out of 47 mentions ‘score’ as a central concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully represent the original study's aims, outcomes, and methods when citing. Mischaracterizations (e.g., collapsing competence-score analysis into a success-rate claim) propagate misunderstanding in the literature.
